strings.prompt.base:
You are an assistant that helps non-expert people understand their Mac.
Always answer in English, with short, clear sentences and no technical jargon.
Rely only on the data provided: do not invent numbers, programs or causes.
If you are not sure about something, say so clearly instead of making it up.
Never say you closed programs or changed settings: you can only explain.
macOS background tasks are part of the system: never suggest quitting them.
strings.slow.topcpu.info: “{0}” is working hard, but the Mac still has power to spare
strings.slow.topcpu.system: macOS is doing some work in the background (“{0}”)
strings.slow.topcpu.system.advice: Wait a few minutes: it usually finishes by itself. If it goes on for hours, restart the Mac.
strings.slow.topcpu.app: “{0}” is using a lot of the processor
strings.slow.topcpu.app.advice: If you don't need it right now, quit “{0}” (save your work first).
strings.slow.mem.advice: Quit the apps and browser tabs you're not using.
strings.slow.swap: The Mac is using the disk as extra memory ({0})
strings.slow.swap.advice: When you can, restart the Mac: it frees up memory.
strings.slow.topmem: “{0}” is using a lot of memory ({1})
strings.slow.topmem.advice: If you don't need it, quit “{0}” to free up memory.
strings.slow.heat.critical: The Mac is very hot and is slowing itself down for protection
strings.slow.heat.warning: The Mac is hot and may slow down to cool off
strings.slow.heat.advice: Put the Mac on a hard surface and keep the air vents clear.
strings.slow.uptime: The Mac hasn't been restarted in {0} days
strings.slow.uptime.advice: Restart the Mac: that's often enough to make it fast again.
strings.slow.prompt.notes: What some macOS background tasks are:
strings.slow.prompt.end:
Explain in 2 or 3 simple sentences what is happening, starting from the problems found.
Only talk about the programs named above. If there are no problems, reassure the user.
Don't give advice and don't make lists: the app already shows the advice.
strings.process.close.macos: Don't quit it: the system needs it
strings.process.close.macos.advice: If it keeps using a lot of processor for hours, restart the Mac.
strings.process.close.app: You can quit it whenever you want
strings.process.close.app.advice: To quit it: save your work, then press ⌘Q while you're in the app.
strings.process.close.component: Don't quit it on its own: if needed, quit “{0}”
strings.process.close.component.advice: To quit “{0}”: save your work, then press ⌘Q while you're in the app.
strings.process.kind.background: It's a background program installed by another app
strings.process.close.background: Only quit it if you know what it's for: it often restarts by itself
strings.process.close.background.advice: You can see and turn off background programs in System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions.
strings.process.kind.unknown: I can't tell where it comes from
strings.process.close.unknown: Better not to quit it if you don't know what it is
strings.process.usage: It's using {0} of the processor and {1} of memory right now
strings.process.prompt.kind.component: it's an internal component of the “{0}” app
strings.process.prompt.kind.background: it's a background program installed by a third party
strings.process.prompt.path: Path (only to understand it, don't mention it): {0}
strings.process.prompt.end:
Explain in 2 or 3 simple sentences what this process is for.
Use the reliable information if there is any; otherwise infer it from the name and, if you're not sure, say so.
Don't say whether it can be quit: the app already shows that. Don't make lists.
strings.process.notfound.known: “{0}” is part of macOS: {1}. Don't quit it.
strings.process.notfound: I can't find “{0}” among the running processes. Check the name: you can copy it from Activity Monitor.
strings.disk.label.systemAssets: Resources downloaded by macOS (voices, fonts, dictionaries…)
strings.disk.label.otherAIModels: AI models from other apps (e.g. Ollama, LM Studio)
strings.disk.label.other: Other apps' data and loose files
strings.disk.advice.appleAI: If you don't use Apple Intelligence, you can turn it off in System Settings → Apple Intelligence & Siri: macOS can then free up part of this space (this app uses it for its explanations, though).
strings.disk.advice.downloads: Look in your Downloads folder: there are often installers and archives you no longer need.
strings.disk.advice.trash: Empty the Trash: right-click the Trash icon in the Dock → Empty Trash.
strings.disk.advice.applications: Delete apps you no longer use: drag them from the Applications folder to the Trash.
strings.disk.advice.pictures: If you use iCloud Photos, you can turn on “Optimize Mac Storage” in Photos → Settings → iCloud.
strings.disk.advice.files: Large files you rarely use can be moved to an external drive or to iCloud Drive.
strings.disk.advice.caches: Caches shouldn't be deleted by hand: macOS frees them up by itself when space runs low.
strings.disk.advice.iosBackups: You can delete old backups from the Finder: select the device → Manage Backups.
strings.disk.advice.otherAIModels: These are models downloaded by apps like Ollama or LM Studio: delete the ones you don't use from the app itself.
strings.disk.advice.developer: If you use Xcode: old simulators and build files can be removed in Xcode → Settings → Components.
strings.disk.advice.swap: Virtual memory shrinks by itself when you restart the Mac.
strings.disk.free.plenty: You still have plenty of free space: no need to free any up now.
strings.disk.free.low: Press “Clean Up” to choose files to remove (they go to the Trash, so you can get them back).
strings.disk.purgeable: macOS frees up another {0} by itself when needed
strings.disk.snapshots.advice: macOS deletes snapshots by itself after about 24 hours or when space is needed.
strings.disk.prompt.plenty: there is plenty of free space
strings.disk.prompt:
User's question: {0}

Disk: {1} free of {2} ({3}).
Biggest items (measured by the app):
{4}

Reliable information:
- In System Settings → General → Storage, “System Data” collects everything that isn't in the other categories: Apple Intelligence models, caches, virtual memory, Time Machine snapshots, app data. On this Mac it's about {5}.
- The Apple Intelligence models are needed for the AI features that run on the Mac.
- macOS frees up caches and snapshots by itself when space is needed.

Explain in 2 or 3 simple sentences where the space went, starting from the biggest items.
If “System Data” is large, explain what it is.
Don't give advice and don't make lists: the app already shows the advice.
strings.health.overall.ok: Your Mac is in good shape
strings.health.speed.bad.advice: Press “Slow Mac” to see what is slowing it down.
strings.health.speed.ok: The Mac is not under strain
strings.health.disk.low.advice: Press “Disk Space” to see what takes up the most space.
strings.health.backup.none.advice: Connect an external drive and turn on Time Machine in System Settings → General → Time Machine: if the Mac breaks, you won't lose your files.
strings.health.backup.old.advice: Connect your Time Machine drive to make an up-to-date backup.
strings.health.filevault.off.advice: Turn on FileVault in System Settings → Privacy & Security: if you lose the Mac, nobody will be able to read your files.
strings.health.gatekeeper.off: The security check for downloaded apps (Gatekeeper) is turned off
strings.health.gatekeeper.off.advice: Gatekeeper can only be turned back on with a Terminal command: if you didn't turn it off yourself, get help from a technician.
strings.health.sip.off: System file protection (SIP) is turned off
strings.health.sip.off.advice: SIP can only be turned back on from the Mac's Recovery mode: if you didn't turn it off yourself, get help from a technician.
strings.health.firewall.off: The firewall is off (macOS's default setting)
strings.health.firewall.off.advice: If you often use public Wi‑Fi networks, you can turn it on in System Settings → Network → Firewall.
strings.health.apps.one: There is 1 app or program to check
strings.health.apps.many: There are {0} apps or programs to check
strings.health.apps.advice: Press “Suspicious Apps” to see what they are and how to remove them.
strings.health.updates.pending.advice: Install the updates in System Settings → General → Software Update: they fix security problems.
strings.health.updates.auto.off.advice: Turn them on in System Settings → General → Software Update → Automatic Updates.
strings.health.battery.worn: The battery is worn ({0}% of its original capacity)
strings.health.battery.worn.advice: Below 80%, Apple recommends having it checked by a service provider.
strings.health.uptime: You haven't restarted the Mac in {0} days
strings.health.uptime.advice: Restart the Mac now and then: it installs updates and frees up memory.
strings.chat.instructions:
You help people use their Mac (macOS {0}). Answer questions about how to do things.
When several actions are needed, use short numbered steps (at most 5).
Use the English names of menus, keys and settings (e.g. System Settings, Finder, Trash).
If you receive a “verified guide”, follow it: it is correct.
Copy keyboard shortcuts EXACTLY as they are written in the guide, with all the symbols (⌘ ⇧ ⌥ ⌃).
If you are not sure where a setting is, say so and suggest searching for it in the System Settings search field or with Spotlight (⌘ Space).
Answer directly, without preamble.
Only if the question has nothing to do with computers and technology, answer in one sentence that you can only help with the Mac.
strings.chat.noGuide: (Note: there is no verified guide for this question. Do not invent names of menus, buttons or icons. If you don't know the steps for sure, explain in one sentence where to look: the search field at the top of System Settings, or the app's Help menu. If the question isn't about computers and technology, just answer that you can only help with the Mac.)
strings.message.prompt:
The user received this message on their Mac and asks what it means:
“{0}”
strings.message.prompt.scam: It's a scam: tell the user clearly and don't give any instructions for following the message.
strings.message.prompt.end: Explain in 2 or 3 simple sentences what the message means. Don't give advice as a list: the app already shows it. Never suggest Terminal commands and never suggest turning off security protections. If the text is incomprehensible or isn't a Mac message, say so.
strings.message.empty: I didn't find any text to explain. Take a screenshot of the message with ⌃⇧⌘4 (it goes to the clipboard) and try again.
strings.security.broken: It happens when a file is changed after it was signed: sometimes it's harmless (apps created by other programs, like developer tools), sometimes not.
strings.security.remove: You can turn it off in System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions (the “Allow in the Background” section). If it comes from an app you don't use, uninstall the app.
strings.security.bg.unwanted.advice: It's a program that shows ads or fake alarms. {0}
strings.security.bg.broken: “{0}” has a digital signature that no longer matches the program
strings.security.bg.script: “{0}” starts by itself and runs a script
strings.security.bg.script.advice: Scripts started in the background are a trick used by adware. If you don't know what it is: {0}
strings.security.bg.hidden: “{0}” starts by itself from a hidden or temporary folder
strings.security.bg.hidden.advice: Legitimate programs don't install themselves there. {0}
strings.security.bg.missing: “{0}” points to a program that no longer exists
strings.security.bg.missing.advice: It's a leftover from an uninstalled app: it's harmless, but you can remove it. {0}
strings.security.bg.unverified: “{0}” starts by itself and no verified developer signs it
strings.security.bg.unverified.advice: If you don't know where it comes from: {0}
strings.security.app.unwanted.advice: It shows fake alarms to make you pay. Uninstall it: drag it from the Applications folder to the Trash and empty it.
strings.security.app.broken: “{0}” has a digital signature that no longer matches the app
strings.security.app.broken.advice: {0} If you don't recognize it, delete it; if you need it, download it again from the official website.
strings.security.app.unverified: “{0}” isn't signed by a verified developer
strings.security.app.unverified.advice: If you downloaded it yourself from an official website (some free programs aren't signed), that's fine. If you don't know where it comes from, delete it.
strings.security.bgcount.none: No program from other companies starts by itself in the background
strings.security.bgcount: Programs that start by themselves in the background: {0}

strings.ui.welcome.what: Ask me questions about your Mac: why it's slow, what a process is, where your space went, how to do something. I can also check it in one click, explain a strange message and alert you if something's wrong.

guides.text: Screenshots: ⌘⇧3 captures the whole screen; ⌘⇧4 a part (drag to select); ⌘⇧4 then Space captures a window; ⌘⇧5 opens the panel with all the options. The images are saved on the Desktop.
Recording the screen: press ⌘⇧5 and choose “Record Entire Screen” or “Record Selected Portion”. To stop, click the stop button in the menu bar.
An app that isn't responding: press ⌥⌘Esc, choose the app and click “Force Quit”. Unsaved changes in that app will be lost.
Searching: press ⌘ Space to open Spotlight and type the name of the file, app or setting.
Uninstalling an app: open the Applications folder in the Finder and drag the app to the Trash (or right-click → Move to Trash), then empty the Trash.
Hidden files: in the Finder press ⌘⇧. (period) to show or hide them.
Copy and paste: ⌘C copies, ⌘X cuts (in text), ⌘V pastes. To move a file in the Finder: ⌘C on the file, then ⌥⌘V in the destination folder.
Emoji: press the 🌐 (Fn) key + E, or ⌃⌘Space.
Renaming a file: select it in the Finder, press Return, type the new name and press Return again.
Compressing: right-click the file or folder → “Compress”. To open a .zip file, just double-click it.
Updating macOS: System Settings → General → Software Update. App Store apps are updated from the App Store.
Backing up with Time Machine: connect an external drive, then System Settings → General → Time Machine → “Add Backup Disk”.
Battery: System Settings → Battery shows the battery health and how much power the apps use.
Seeing the Wi‑Fi password: System Settings → Wi‑Fi → “Details…” next to the network → “Copy Password”.
Dark mode: System Settings → Appearance → Light, Dark or Auto.
Bigger text: System Settings → Displays → choose a “Larger Text” resolution. In the browser and many apps press ⌘+ (Command and plus) to zoom in and ⌘− (Command and minus) to zoom out.
Tiling windows: hover over the green button at the top left of the window and choose a layout, or drag the window to the edge of the screen.
Apps at startup: System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions; remove with “−” the apps you don't want when the Mac starts.
Changing the app that opens a type of file: right-click the file → Get Info → “Open with” → choose the app → “Change All…”.
AirDrop: right-click the file → Share → AirDrop, then choose the device. The nearby device needs Wi‑Fi and Bluetooth turned on.
Connecting a Bluetooth device: put it in pairing mode, then System Settings → Bluetooth → “Connect” next to the device.
Dictation: turn it on in System Settings → Keyboard → Dictation; then press the microphone key (or press Fn twice) and speak.
More desktops: open Mission Control (F3 or swipe up with three fingers) and click “+” at the top right.
Printing: ⌘P. Adding a printer: System Settings → Printers & Scanners → “Add Printer, Scanner or Fax…”.
Changing the wallpaper: System Settings → Wallpaper, then choose a picture. You can also right-click a picture in the Finder → “Set Desktop Picture”.
Screen saver: System Settings → Screen Saver.
Notifications: System Settings → Notifications, then choose the app to decide if and how its notifications appear.

Audio: System Settings → Sound to choose output, input and volume; the alert sound is chosen in the “Sound Effects” section of the same page. You can also change the volume from Control Center in the menu bar.
Downloaded files: they're in the Downloads folder. In the Finder click “Downloads” in the sidebar, or press ⌥⌘L.
The Mac's name: System Settings → General → About, then edit the “Name” field.
Second monitor: connect the cable (USB‑C/Thunderbolt or HDMI) and the Mac recognizes it by itself. To arrange the screens or choose the main one: System Settings → Displays.
Connecting to Wi‑Fi: click the Wi‑Fi icon in the menu bar (or in Control Center), choose the network and enter the password. Networks are managed in System Settings → Wi‑Fi.
The Mac's password: System Settings → Users & Groups → click the “i” button next to your name, then use the button next to “Password”. You'll need the current password.
Locking the screen: press ⌃⌘Q, or Apple menu () at the top left → “Lock Screen”. You'll need your password to get back in.
Shutting down, restarting or sleeping: Apple menu () at the top left → “Shut Down…”, “Restart…” or “Sleep”.
Symbols on a US keyboard: @ is ⇧2; # is ⇧3; € is ⌥⇧2; ~ is ⇧` (the key to the left of 1). Other keyboard layouts put them elsewhere: check System Settings → Keyboard → Text Input.

Essential shortcuts: ⌘Z undoes the last action (⌘⇧Z redoes it); ⌘A selects all; ⌘W closes the window; ⌘Q quits the app; ⌘Tab switches between apps (hold ⌘ and press Tab several times). The red button to close a window is at the top left.
Screen brightness: use the keys with the sun on the keyboard (F1 and F2), or Control Center in the menu bar → Display, or System Settings → Displays.
The Mac's language: System Settings → General → Language & Region; add the language with “+” and drag it to the top of the list. A restart is needed to apply it everywhere.
Emptying the Trash: right-click the Trash icon in the Dock → “Empty Trash”.

Opening an app: press ⌘ Space, type the app's name (e.g. Terminal) and press Return. Or open Applications in the Finder; system apps like Terminal and Activity Monitor are in Applications → Utilities.

processes.kernel_task: the heart of macOS; when it uses a lot of processor it is often slowing the Mac down on purpose to cool it
processes.launchd: starts and manages all the other macOS processes
processes.loginwindow: manages login and the user session; quitting it logs you out
processes.WindowServer: draws everything you see on screen; it works harder with many displays or windows
processes.configd: manages the network and system configuration
processes.runningboardd: decides how many resources each app gets
processes.UserEventAgent: reacts to system events (e.g. connecting a device)
processes.fseventsd: keeps track of file changes, for Time Machine and Spotlight
processes.diskarbitrationd: manages connected disks and USB drives
processes.Finder: the app for browsing files and folders; if you quit it, it reopens by itself
processes.Dock: the Dock and full-screen window management
processes.SystemUIServer: some of the icons in the menu bar
processes.ControlCenter: Control Center and some menu bar icons
processes.mds: Spotlight indexing your files; it usually calms down by itself after a while
processes.mds_stores: Spotlight indexing your files; it usually calms down by itself after a while
processes.mdworker_shared: Spotlight reading files for search; temporary
processes.photoanalysisd: Photos analyzing your pictures (faces, objects); it works when the Mac is idle
processes.mediaanalysisd: analyzes photos and videos for search; it works when the Mac is idle
processes.suggestd: prepares suggestions (e.g. contacts and events found in Mail and Messages)
processes.nsurlsessiond: background downloads and uploads for apps and the system
processes.rapportd: communication between your Apple devices (Handoff, Continuity)
processes.softwareupdated: checking for or downloading macOS updates
processes.trustd: checks the security certificates of websites and apps
processes.syspolicyd: security check for apps you just opened or downloaded
processes.modelmanagerd: manages the Apple Intelligence AI models
processes.TGOnDeviceInferenceProviderService: runs the Apple Intelligence model on the Mac (this app uses it too)
processes.com.apple.WebKit.WebContent: the web pages open in Safari or other apps

messages.title: This is almost certainly a SCAM
messages.advice: macOS never shows virus warnings inside the browser and Apple never asks you to call a number. Don't call, don't download anything and don't give out passwords: close the tab with ⌘W (if it won't close, quit the browser with ⌥⌘Esc).

messages.title: It's a macOS security check on apps downloaded from the internet
messages.advice: If the app comes from an official website you trust, you can open it from System Settings → Privacy & Security: scroll down and press “Open Anyway”. If you don't know where it comes from, delete it.

patterns: is damaged and should be moved
messages.title: macOS is blocking an app that looks damaged or tampered with
messages.advice: Delete the app and download it again from the official website or the App Store. Don't use commands found online to force it open.

messages.title: Disk space is running out
messages.advice: Press “Disk Space” in this app to see what takes up the most space.

messages.title: The Mac has run out of memory for apps
messages.advice: Quit the apps and browser tabs you're not using. If it happens often, press “Slow Mac” in this app.

messages.title: An app has frozen
messages.advice: Press ⌥⌘Esc, choose the app and click “Force Quit”. Unsaved changes in that app will be lost.

patterns: shut down because of a problem
messages.title: The Mac restarted by itself because of an error
messages.advice: If it happened only once, don't worry. If it happens again: install the macOS and app updates, disconnect accessories and, if it continues, contact Apple Support.

messages.title: An app is asking for a permission
messages.advice: Only allow it if you know the app and the permission makes sense for what it does (e.g. a video-call app and the camera). You can change your mind in System Settings → Privacy & Security.

messages.title: The keychain is asking for your password
messages.advice: The keychain stores your passwords: it usually asks for the same password you use to log in to the Mac. Only enter it if the request comes from an app you're using.

messages.title: macOS is asking whether to trust a connected accessory
messages.advice: Allow it if you just connected that accessory yourself (USB drive, disk, adapter). If you didn't connect anything, don't allow it.

messages.title: Your iCloud storage is full (it's online, not on the Mac)
messages.advice: You can see what takes up iCloud in System Settings → your name → iCloud. Freeing up space on the Mac doesn't fix this message.

cleanup: what can i get rid of
